strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question by systematically adapting Mamba to HuBERT-style speech self-supervised learning, covering causal and bidirectional models, ASR, computational efficiency, representation probing, and downstream tasks.

The efficiency analysis provides useful evidence that Mamba-based models have near-constant MACs per second with respect to sequence length and can process long documents where the same-size Transformer encounters out-of-memory errors.

The long-context ASR experiment is practically relevant: ExtBiMamba improves TEDLIUM3 document-level WER from 13.37% to 11.08% when full-document context is used, and the improvement is statistically tested.
The causal ASR result is promising: a smaller 78.2M-parameter Mamba model achieves 15.77% WER versus 16.66% for a 94.7M-parameter causal Transformer.

The representation analysis is broad, combining layer-wise phone purity, CCA with phonetic, speaker, and emotion labels, and downstream probing, and the paper honestly reports that bidirectional Mamba does not dominate at every scale.
The ablation comparing ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba provides actionable evidence that the optimal bidirectional Mamba design depends on model size.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet adequate. The manuscript does not clearly state the pretraining corpus and splits, model dimensions, Mamba state and kernel settings, optimizer and schedule, masking configuration, fine-tuning hyperparameters, random seeds, or code/model release plans.

The fairness of the main comparisons is under-specified. All models are trained with a reduced global batch under a single-GPU resource constraint, but the paper does not show that this setup is equally suitable for Mamba and Transformer training or compare against standard well-trained HuBERT baselines.

Most results appear to come from single runs without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The one paired t-test does not include multiple-comparison correction, and the ASR and SUPERB differences are often small enough that run-to-run variance could change conclusions.

The efficiency evidence needs clarification. The RTF axis is unusually scaled and labeled, measured values are called Real-Time Factor despite being in the hundreds, and the causal Transformer is reported to OOM beyond 80 seconds while a bidirectional Transformer appears to run to 320 seconds. Batch size, precision, memory usage, and implementation details should also be reported.

The long-context superiority claim is limited by the absence of a competitive memory-efficient Transformer baseline, such as chunked attention, linear attention, or gradient-checkpointed Transformer. The only same-size Transformer fails with OOM, so there is no direct document-level quality comparison.

The streaming-ASR claim is based on one narrow comparison and only a 0.89 absolute WER difference; because the Mamba model also has about 17% fewer parameters, parameter count and architecture are confounded. Matched-parameter models and additional datasets are needed.

Although described as SUPERB evaluation, only four MiniSUPERB tasks are used. The aggregate score is not fully explained, can obscure task-level tradeoffs, and the base bidirectional Transformer substantially outperforms ExtBiMamba, so claims of broad downstream competitiveness should be softened.

Phone purity and CCA do not establish 'higher-quality quantized representations' by themselves. They are diagnostic correlations and can depend on clustering geometry and layer choice; the paper itself notes their mismatch with downstream performance, making the abstract-level claim too strong.
The novelty over very recent Mamba-based speech SSL work, especially references [16] and [17], should be more sharply delineated to justify the 'first comprehensive exploration' claim.

There are several presentation issues, including typographical errors such as 'probling' and 'phenomenon,' dense figures, and the phrase 'In conclusion' appearing before the contribution list in the introduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: whether Mamba/state-space backbones can serve as full HuBERT-style speech self-supervised models rather than only as components in isolated speech tasks.
The evaluation is broad, combining computational efficiency, long-context and causal ASR, phone purity, CCA representation analysis, SUPERB probing, and a bidirectional Mamba ablation.
The Mamba and Transformer models are trained from scratch under the same HuBERT procedure, which provides a useful within-paper comparison despite the reduced overall training scale.

The efficiency results are consistent with Mamba's theoretical linear-time scaling: MACs per second remain nearly flat as sequence length increases, whereas dense Transformer attention grows quadratically.

The long-context experiment demonstrates a practical feasibility advantage in the authors' setup: ExtBiMamba can process full TED talks while the dense Transformer baseline encounters out-of-memory errors.

The causal results are encouraging, with the 78.2M-parameter Mamba model achieving 15.77% WER against 16.66% for the 94.7M-parameter causal Transformer, and the bidirectional ablation offers useful size-dependent design guidance.
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly equates causal masking with streaming ASR, but no online or streaming evaluation is provided. There are no chunking, latency, lookahead, state-recurrence, endpoint-detection, or real-time deployment experiments, so the streaming claim should be removed or substantiated.

ASR evidence is centered on TEDLIUM3 and lacks multi-dataset generality, multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main WER comparisons. The reported 15.77 versus 16.66 WER difference may not be reliable without such analysis.

The long-context claim is stronger than the evidence supports. The only failing baseline is a vanilla dense Transformer; there is no comparison with FlashAttention, memory-efficient attention, sliding-window attention, chunked attention, or other scalable Transformer variants. Thus the result demonstrates an advantage over one implementation, not over Transformers generally.

The document-level ASR experiment lacks important details about decoding, CTC configuration, the appended convolutional encoder, tokenization, language models, and how document-level segmentation and scoring were handled.

The efficiency study is incomplete. Peak GPU memory is not directly measured despite the central OOM claim, and batch size, precision, warmup, kernel implementation, and Mamba/attention software versions are not reported. The RTF figure is also confusing: its axis direction and apparent trends are difficult to reconcile with the statement that RTF increases with sequence length.

The claim of higher-quality quantized representations rests mainly on phone purity. The paper does not report cluster balance, mutual information, alternative clustering metrics, or an actual spoken-language-model downstream use of those units. CCA details such as regularization, component selection, cross-validation, and statistical significance are also missing.

The SUPERB analysis uses only four tasks, and the resulting four-task aggregate score should not be interpreted as comprehensive SUPERB performance. The results are mixed: the base bidirectional Transformer substantially outperforms ExtBiMamba, while the small standard Mamba is slightly below the causal Transformer in aggregate score.

Architectural fairness is not fully resolved. The default Mamba block omits the feed-forward MLP used in Transformer blocks, and several comparisons use different parameter counts; for example, small Mamba+MLP has 33.0M parameters versus 23.5M for the causal Transformer. Mamba+MLP ASR results would clarify the source of the gains.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the current version. Key pretraining data and hyperparameters, masking configuration, optimizer and schedule, positional encoding choices, Mamba configuration, downstream-head settings, random seeds, and code/model release are not specified.

The novelty is primarily empirical and incremental relative to concurrent Mamba speech-SSL work, and the claim that this is the 'first comprehensive' exploration needs sharper differentiation from prior studies. In its current form, the paper does not meet the Findings soundness and reproducibility bar without important revisions.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and broad empirical exploration of Mamba as a drop-in replacement for Transformer blocks in HuBERT, covering computational efficiency, long-context ASR, causal/streaming ASR, representation probing, CCA analyses, and bidirectional architecture ablations.

The central efficiency claim is well motivated: Mamba's linear-time complexity is reflected in nearly sequence-length-independent MACs, while the Transformer baselines grow rapidly and fail under full-document inputs. The document-level ExtBiMamba result (11.08% WER versus Transformer OOM) demonstrates a practical advantage for long-context processing.

The causal ASR comparison is promising: Mamba obtains 15.77% WER with 78.2M parameters, compared with 16.66% for the 94.7M-parameter Causal Transformer. The use of the same HuBERT training pipeline and from-scratch Transformer controls also improves comparability.

The analysis goes beyond end-task scores by examining phone purity and CCA similarity to phonetic, speaker, and emotion embeddings. The stronger phone purity and speaker-related similarity of causal Mamba representations are useful findings.

The authors are commendably transparent about mixed results, especially that base-size bidirectional Mamba remains below the Transformer on SUPERB and that the optimal ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba design depends on model scale.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not specify several essential details, including the pretraining corpus and hours, model dimensions, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, masking configuration, fine-tuning hyperparameters, decoding setup, random seeds, and inference kernel/precision settings. The reduced single-GPU pretraining recipe could also affect all downstream comparisons.

Figure 1 is confusing as rendered: the RTF axis runs from 400 to 1800, while the text states that lower RTF is better, making the relative positions of Mamba and Transformer difficult to interpret. The reported OOM behavior beyond 80 seconds also appears to conflict with measurements plotted up to 320 seconds. The metric should be clearly defined as RTF or throughput, and peak-memory results should be reported.

Several comparisons are not fully capacity-controlled. The causal ASR Mamba has 78.2M parameters versus 94.7M for the Transformer, and some small-scale SUPERB comparisons use 23.5M versus 33.0M parameters. A matched-parameter Mamba+MLP ASR result and multiple pretraining/fine-tuning seeds would strengthen the conclusions. Most task differences lack confidence intervals or significance tests.

The long-context evidence is based primarily on TEDLIUM3 and depends on the chosen memory setup. The Transformer is stronger at utterance level (11.86% versus 13.37%), and no memory-efficient Transformer baseline is included. Thus, the result establishes an advantage for unsegmented full-document processing under the tested configuration, not general ASR superiority.

The downstream evaluation uses only four MiniSUPERB tasks rather than the full SUPERB benchmark, despite the abstract's broader wording. Moreover, base-size ExtBiMamba substantially underperforms the Transformer (815.38 versus 868.93 SUPERB_S), and even the stronger InnBiMamba+MLP does not close this gap, limiting the evidence for bidirectional scalability.

Some representational claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Higher phone purity or CCA similarity does not necessarily imply better general representations, as the authors themselves note when purity does not align with downstream performance. ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba are also mainly defined by citation, making the architecture less self-contained.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and reasonably comprehensive empirical study of Mamba as a drop-in replacement for Transformer blocks in HuBERT, while controlling much of the surrounding training pipeline and feature-extraction frontend.

The efficiency evidence is compelling: Mamba-based models maintain nearly constant MACs per second and substantially lower RTF as sequence length grows, whereas Transformer costs increase sharply and encounter OOM limitations.

The long-context ASR study demonstrates a practical advantage: ExtBiMamba can process full TEDLIUM3 documents and improves WER from 13.37% at utterance level to 11.08% at document level, with a reported statistically significant context benefit.

In the causal setting, the smaller 78.2M-parameter Mamba model achieves 15.77% WER compared with 16.66% for the 94.7M-parameter Causal Transformer, and Mamba variants also show strong phonetic and speaker-related probing results.

The analysis is broad, combining ASR, phone purity, CCA against phonetic/speaker/emotion labels, SUPERB probing, bidirectional architecture ablations, full-benchmark results, and training-dynamics analysis. The authors are transparent about ExtBiMamba's base-scale weaknesses and instability.
Code is promised, and the single-GPU setup, model configurations, and training procedure are described in enough detail to make the study substantially reproducible.
weaknesses: Most main results come from a single pretraining run without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or variance estimates. This is a significant limitation when several SUPERB and WER differences are small and architecture rankings are size-dependent.

The single-GPU setup uses a smaller effective batch and roughly one quarter of the audio per step seen in the original HuBERT setting. Although the internal comparison is fair, external validity and behavior at conventional training scale remain uncertain.

Some comparisons are not parameter- or component-matched: causal Mamba is 78.2M versus 94.7M for the Transformer, while small Mamba+MLP is 33.0M versus 23.5M for competing models. The default Mamba block also lacks a feed-forward MLP, so claims of superiority should be more carefully qualified.

The broad abstract claim that Mamba produces higher-quality quantized representations and captures speaker features more distinctly than Transformer-based models is only partially supported. The advantage depends on layer, model size, causal versus bidirectional setting, and evaluation metric.

The bidirectional results weaken the case for Mamba as a general HuBERT replacement: the Base Transformer outperforms ExtBiMamba across all four probing tasks and in the full SUPERB evaluation, while ExtBiMamba also exhibits persistent training instability.

For long-context ASR, no same-size Transformer document-level result is available because of OOM. The experiment therefore establishes Mamba's feasibility and benefit from context, but not document-level accuracy superiority over a Transformer; at utterance level the Transformer is actually better.

Several analytical details are underspecified, including the data and sampling used for CCA, speaker/emotion embedding versions, clustering implementation, the unit of comparison for the paired t-test, and random seeds. Appendix C also inconsistently refers to slot filling rather than the intent-classification task used in the main tables.
The conceptual contribution is primarily an empirical architecture substitution and evaluation rather than a new modeling method, so its broader impact is moderate despite its practical relevance.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question by replacing Transformer blocks in the HuBERT pipeline with Mamba variants while retaining the same CNN frontend, pretraining procedure, and downstream evaluation framework.

It provides a broad empirical investigation spanning computational scaling, long-context ASR, causal/streaming ASR, layer-wise phone purity, CCA-based representation analysis, four-task SUPERB probing, full SUPERB results, bidirectional architecture ablations, and training stability.

The efficiency evidence supports the main architectural motivation: Mamba-based models exhibit nearly constant MACs per second as sequence length grows, whereas Transformer computation grows sharply, and Mamba can process document-level speech under a setting where the causal Transformer encounters out-of-memory errors.

The causal results are promising: the 78.2M-parameter Mamba model obtains 15.77% WER against 16.66% for the 94.7M-parameter causal Transformer, and Mamba variants perform strongly on several causal SUPERB tasks, especially phoneme and speaker-related evaluation.

The authors report mixed outcomes rather than only favorable ones, including weaker bidirectional performance at Base scale, ExtBiMamba training instability, and scale-dependent differences between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba. These negative findings are useful for future speech SSM design.
weaknesses: Statistical robustness is limited. Each pretraining configuration appears to use a single run, with no random seeds, confidence intervals, or run-to-run variance. Several SUPERB differences are below one point, and the only significance test compares document- and utterance-level results within ExtBiMamba rather than across architectures.

Several key performance comparisons are not fully parameter- or component-matched. Causal ASR compares a 78.2M Mamba without a feed-forward MLP against a 94.7M Transformer, and the Small Mamba+MLP model has 33.0M parameters versus 23.5M for its Transformer baseline. This makes claims about architecture-level superiority less decisive.

The wall-clock efficiency evidence is difficult to validate as presented. Figure 1 uses an RTF axis whose direction and convention appear inconsistent with the text, which says Mamba has lower RTF while the plotted numerical trend suggests the opposite. The paper should clarify the RTF definition, axis orientation, inference batch size, precision, kernels, and memory settings.

The long-context experiment demonstrates feasibility more clearly than accuracy superiority. The Transformer wins the utterance-level comparison, 11.86% versus 13.37% WER, but cannot be evaluated at document level under the chosen memory budget; no memory-efficient Transformer baseline such as checkpointing, FlashAttention, or chunked attention is included.

Reproducibility is not fully adequate in the submitted version: the abstract states that code is available but no URL is shown, downstream fine-tuning configurations and seeds are underspecified, and the main SUPERB setup uses intent classification while Appendix C describes slot filling in the score formula.

The representation analyses are correlational and lack uncertainty estimates. Higher phone purity or CCA similarity does not consistently imply better downstream phoneme probing, so claims that Mamba captures speaker or phonetic information more distinctly should be interpreted cautiously.

The methodological novelty is primarily an architecture substitution and empirical survey. The paper does not directly compare against recent Mamba-based speech SSL systems or hybrid Mamba–Transformer models, and the claim of being the first comprehensive exploration is stronger than the related-work evidence supports.

External validity remains limited by the reduced single-GPU pretraining setup, one main pretraining corpus, and a small number of ASR datasets. The observed bidirectional scaling problems may therefore reflect either the architecture or the particular training regime.

strengths: Timely and reasonably comprehensive empirical exploration of Mamba as a drop-in replacement for Transformer blocks in HuBERT, covering causal and bidirectional models, ASR, long-context processing, representation analysis, SUPERB probing, and architecture ablations.

The efficiency evidence is practically relevant: Mamba-based models maintain nearly sequence-length-independent MACs, achieve lower RTF for long sequences, and avoid the out-of-memory failures encountered by causal Transformer HuBERT beyond roughly 80 seconds.

The long-context and causal ASR results are compelling. ExtBiMamba improves WER from 13.37% at utterance level to 11.08% at document level on TEDLIUM3, while a 78.2M-parameter causal Mamba model reaches 15.77% WER versus 16.66% for a 94.7M causal Transformer.

The study goes beyond end-to-end ASR with phone purity, canonical-correlation analysis, SUPERB probing, and full SUPERB results, giving a multifaceted view of what Mamba representations do well, especially phonetic and speaker-related information.

The authors report unfavorable results honestly: bidirectional ExtBiMamba underperforms the Transformer at Base scale, Mamba lags on several paralinguistic/semantic tasks, and ExtBiMamba exhibits training instability. This nuance makes the central claims more credible.

Reproducibility is supported by detailed training settings, named datasets and baselines, hardware information, repeated RTF measurements, ablations, and appendices; the promised code release would further strengthen this.
weaknesses: The main pretraining and downstream comparisons appear to rely on single training runs, with no seed variation, confidence intervals, or statistical tests except for the long-context ASR comparison. Several performance gaps are modest, so training variance could affect the conclusions.

The models are trained in a reduced single-GPU regime with substantially less total audio per batch than the original HuBERT setup. Although the same setup is used for the internal baselines, it may not be equally optimal for Mamba and Transformer, and it limits claims about scalability to larger models or official-scale training.

The conclusion that Mamba has limited bidirectional scalability may partly reflect optimization instability rather than an inherent architectural limitation. The loss-scale analysis supports this concern, but alternative learning rates, warmups, initialization, or hybrid/normalization designs are not explored.

Efficiency results are measured on one hardware/software setup and do not compare against memory-efficient, chunked, linear-attention, or otherwise optimized long-context Transformer baselines. The OOM threshold and RTF values may therefore be implementation-dependent.

The long-context evaluation is limited to one dataset and one bidirectional Mamba variant. Since the Transformer cannot process full documents, the experiment demonstrates a practical memory advantage but does not establish how Mamba would compare against a scalable Transformer baseline.

Some reporting details should be cleaned up, including the missing visible code URL after ‘available at’, minor parameter-count inconsistencies such as 94.3M versus 94.7M, and the appendix description of slot filling where the main text reports intent classification. Exact model configurations and total training cost would also improve reproducibility.

The technical contribution is primarily an empirical adaptation and systematic study rather than a new modeling method; combined with the mixed bidirectional results and reduced training scale, this makes the case for main-conference acceptance close rather than unambiguous.
